title: Core Gameplay Loop
summary: Maps the explore-discover-prepare-fight-earn-improve cycle across sessions, long-term progression and rewards.

headings.text: Why does the loop return to the beginning?
Two Loops Working at the Same Time

blocks.text: Short-, medium-, and long-term gameplay loops

Editorial note. An important editorial decision has already been established: the current combat direction is real-time combat. The detailed combat model will be resolved in the Combat System document.
The Core Gameplay Loop of Symphony of Justice represents the primary sequence of actions the player will repeat throughout much of the experience.
Its purpose is to connect exploration, narrative, combat, characters, and progression within a single cycle, preventing these systems from feeling like isolated activities.
The player travels through the different regions of the world in search of objectives, characters, resources, enemies, locations, and events.

During exploration, the player may find main or side missions, materials, hidden areas, NPCs, enemies, dungeons, special activities, historical elements, or information connected to characters and past events.
Exploration should provide two kinds of rewards:
Progression, through resources, items, and access to new activities.
Knowledge, through information that helps the player better understand the world and its inhabitants.
Exploration causes the player to encounter something they did not know before. A strange location, an enemy, a mission, a resource, or a clue creates a new question or objective.
Discovery occurs when the player finds something that gives them a reason to act.
This may be a new character, a mission, an enemy, an important resource, a hidden area, a dungeon, a new route, or an unexpected event.
Not every discovery must lead directly to combat. Some discoveries may reward curiosity through information, items, relationships with characters, or access to new parts of the world.

However, many discoveries will introduce a problem or challenge. The player now understands what they want to obtain or what problem they need to solve. Before confronting it, they may need to analyze the situation and decide which characters and tools to use.
Once the player understands the challenge, they can decide how to approach it. This is where strategic team building becomes relevant.
The player may consider elements such as:
Not every encounter requires extensive preparation, but the player should be able to adapt the party when a challenge justifies doing so.
This reinforces one of the ideas established in the Game Vision: a strong team composition should not depend only on using the individually strongest characters.
Preparation leads to combat or overcoming the challenge.

The player uses the selected characters and tools to resolve the challenge they encountered. Combat should allow the player to use each character's distinctive traits and the interactions between them, progressively incorporating:
The goal is not simply for the player to own characters that are stronger than the enemy. The experience should also reward the player's ability to understand how those characters work together.

In addition, not every challenge must necessarily be resolved through combat. Depending on future content, some situations may be solved through exploration, interaction, investigation, or other systems.
The player receives rewards from combat, exploration, missions, and other activities.
These rewards may include materials, experience, equipment, currency, progression resources, information, access to new areas, new missions, or other content.
Learning something about a character, revealing part of a region's history, or discovering an unknown route can also represent meaningful progress.
The player uses acquired resources to develop characters and tools.
Depending on which systems are ultimately approved, this may include levels, abilities, talents, weapons, equipment, professions, statistics, or different forms of specialization.
The final rules will be defined in the Progression System document.
For the Core Loop, only one principle needs to be established:

Playing should provide resources that expand or strengthen the player's available possibilities. Improvement should not mean only obtaining larger numbers. An upgrade may also unlock new strategies, interactions, or ways of using a character.

The player reorganizes their available options using what they have earned and developed. They may change party members, experiment with new combinations, take advantage of different elements, modify equipment, or discover new synergies.
This step directly answers a question already introduced in the Game Vision:
"What can I build with the characters I have?"

The goal is to prevent the player from finding one team composition early in the game and then having no reason to change it. New challenges and characters should create possibilities rather than simply replacing what existed before.

As a consequence of exploring, fighting, progressing, and developing the party, the player gains access to new possibilities. These may include new territories, missions, chapters, characters, enemies, dungeons, activities, stories, resources, or systems.
Player growth should not only allow them to defeat enemies with larger health pools. It should progressively expand what they can do and what they can discover.
Why does the loop return to the beginning?
Because every new territory, character, mission, or system generates something else to investigate. The player now has:
more knowledge + new tools + new objectives.
The cycle can be represented as follows:
Find locations, resources, characters, and stories.
Find an opportunity, question, or challenge.
Resolve the challenge using the game's systems.
For documents, diagrams, and presentations, the loop can be condensed into:
Explore → Discover → Prepare → Fight → Earn → Improve → Build → Unlock → Explore
For an even more visual version:
EXPLORE → DISCOVER → FIGHT → GROW → BUILD → EXPLORE
Two Loops Working at the Same Time

An especially important aspect of Symphony of Justice is that the player does not progress only by increasing combat power. Knowledge, understanding game mechanics, and learning how to optimize available options also allow the player to overcome increasingly complex challenges.

This connects directly to the pillars already defined in the project: exploration should provide both progression and knowledge, while discovering information may change the player's interpretation of a nation, character, or conflict.
For that reason, the following statement can be preserved as a principle of the Core Gameplay Loop:
In Symphony of Justice, progression means becoming more capable of facing the world while, at the same time, understanding it better.
The Session Loop describes what a player may do during an approximately 20- to 60-minute play session.
Not every session should be identical. Players may enter the game with different objectives depending on their progression and preferences.

The original documentation already includes world missions, exploration, events, and character content, together with enemies, bosses, and special activities. More recent documents also preserve concepts such as hunts, an Adventurers' Guild, and daily missions.
For this reason, a session should allow the player to alternate between activities instead of becoming a mandatory checklist.
When entering the game, the player should quickly be able to identify:
What do I want to achieve now?
What can I meaningfully advance with the time I have available?
The player may continue the story, develop a character, explore a region, complete a mission, search for materials, or overcome a challenge.
A session may combine four major types of activities:
Travel through territories, search for materials, discover routes, NPCs, secrets, and narrative elements.
Normal encounters, elites, bosses, dungeons, hunts, or other activities.
Complete daily missions, make progress on weekly missions, and advance complementary missions or activities connected to the player's current environment and objectives.
Improve characters, review team compositions, equipment, abilities, and resources, and prepare new strategies.
The original documentation also proposed progressive dungeons designed to combine challenge and story, which fits particularly well with medium-length sessions.
A session should be able to end once the player achieves at least one recognizable form of progress.
"Today I advanced something I cared about, and I know what I could do when I return."
A good session should not depend on completing every daily mission.

Daily missions should be easy to complete and have low requirements, allowing the player to satisfy them through normal play. Examples could include logging into the game, spending a resource, upgrading an item, completing a mission, preparing a meal, or participating in a weekly activity.

Daily missions should not interrupt or force the player into specific tasks. Instead, they should be completed naturally as the player chooses activities that feel comfortable or feasible for their own playstyle.

Recurring activities may exist, but they should provide options. This is why activities may be organized on daily, weekly, monthly, or version-based schedules. They should not turn the game into a second job.
Every session should allow meaningful progress even when the player does not participate in every available activity.
The Long-Term Loop explains why a person might continue playing for weeks, months, or years.
This is where the gacha and ongoing-service vision becomes more relevant.

The Game Vision proposes that Symphony of Justice can grow progressively through new regions, characters, stories, systems, and activities. Historical documentation also envisioned a long project lifespan and included events, weekly dungeons, gacha systems, social activities, and expansions.
Retention should therefore be supported by several forms of progression operating at the same time.
The player continues playing to discover:
One of the objectives already established in the Game Vision is to end narrative experiences with answers that create new questions.
"Curiosity is also a form of retention."
Long-term progression should not consist exclusively of increasing statistics. It should also expand what each character can do and what compositions the player can create.
The player may seek characters because of:
gameplay + design + story + personal affinity + team composition.
The Game Vision establishes that obtaining a character should provide both a new strategic tool and a new perspective on the universe.
Gacha may function as one acquisition method, but it should not be the only reason to continue playing.
Historical documentation proposes that additional copies of a character progressively complete a Legacy Card, connecting mechanical growth to an important moment in that character's history.
This system has potential to become part of the Long-Term Loop because it connects:
Its economic rules will still need to be reviewed in the Gacha System document.
There is also a long-term goal that does not necessarily depend on obtaining items: learning to play better.
This allows progression to be more than purely vertical.
Completing certain chapters and requirements may progressively unlock access to:
Expansion should feel like a consequence of progressing through the world, not simply like a list of updates.
Over the long term, the game may incorporate:
These concepts already appear in the historical documentation.
However, recurring content should create variety and anticipation rather than constant pressure.
The player stays because there is still something to discover, someone to develop, and a strategy to master.
The Reward Loop establishes what the player receives after investing time, skill, exploration, or resources. Rewards should feed back into the Core Loop. In other words:
The reward for playing should create new possibilities for continued play.
The original project already includes experience resources for characters, weapons, and talents; nation-specific materials; cosmetics; decoration; and different progression systems.
The rewards can be classified into four categories:
The Legacy Card could function as a hybrid reward because it is currently conceived both as a mechanical expansion of a character and as a representation of part of that character's history.
May reward materials, routes, chests, Codex entries, secrets, encounters, missions, and knowledge.
May reward experience, materials, items, currency, and access to later content.
May provide narrative progression, resources, relationships, unlocks, and knowledge of the world.
May provide more specialized rewards such as equipment, advanced materials, unique resources, or progression related to specific systems.

May provide special stories, themed rewards, cosmetics, resources, and activities with mechanical variations. The original event missions were already intended to introduce variety and reduce monotony.
May primarily provide characters, weapons, or other content defined later.
It should be treated as one branch of the Reward/Acquisition Loop, not as the entire reward system.
In this way, the Reward Loop feeds directly back into the Core Loop.
An important distinction needs to be made here:
The historical documentation does not yet define in sufficient detail what happens when the player loses.

Victory and defeat conditions are contemplated for the current prototype. Because the project is designed as a character-driven gacha RPG, failure is primarily understood as feedback that the current party, progression state, or approach is not yet suited to the challenge, rather than as a reason to punish the player heavily for attempting content.

As a consequence, combat and progression should provide enough information for the player to understand what needs to be improved or reprioritized in a character, such as level, talents, artifacts/equipment, or other relevant progression systems.
The intention is to reduce unnecessary punishment in world exploration or practice environments while still allowing difficult encounters to communicate meaningful requirements.
A useful defeat should communicate information such as:
the main source of incoming damage;

characters, new abilities, talents, specialized equipment
skins, accessories, decorations, profile elements, or housing items
Codex entries, memories, stories, archives, Legacy Cards, scenes, or information
